Let me carefully analyze this write-up against the required mechanisms.

The problem: sequence defined greedily; prove eventual translation periodicity.

Required mechanisms per the grading instructions:

(C) Characterization: an integer $m \ge a_1$ is a term iff its prime support meets the prime support of every term (equivalently every earlier term). This is the standard reduction. Score 2 if written out fully.

(F) Finiteness / large-prime erasure: membership depends only on primes in a finite set (e.g., primes $\le a_1$ or $\le a_1^2$), because any term divisible by a large prime is dominated by a smaller number with same small-prime support that is itself a term — proved for all terms. This is the lower_bound field (used to bound L etc. — actually "lower_bound" here is the finiteness lemma ensuring only finitely many primes matter). Wait, the field mapping says: "lower_bound" = (F) finiteness / large-prime erasure; "upper_bound" = (P) global periodicity from n=1.

Hmm, but actually the field names: lower_bound and upper_bound probably refer to bounding L or the counting T. Anyway follow mapping: lower_bound = (F) finiteness; upper_bound = (P) periodicity assembly.

(P) Periodicity assembly: with L = product of finitely many relevant primes, membership invariant under m -> m+L for every m >= a_1, and T = number of terms in a window of length L, giving a_{n+T} = a_n + L for all n >= 1.

Also: wrong_answer_stated = true if text proves only eventual periodicity or relies on a false lemma (e.g., "each new term's prime support is a minimal hitting set").

Now let's grade the write-up.

The write-up is a "tracking file" with status solved, approaches, and a "Full proof" section.

Section 1: Defines S(m) as set of prime divisors. Characterizes a_{n+1} as minimal > a_n with S(a_{n+1}) intersecting all S_i. Then minimal family M_n (inclusion-minimal members of F_n). Then a claim: "S meets every M_n-member iff meets every S_i" — yes trivially true since each S_i contains a minimal member. Hmm wait, careful: "if S meets every M_n member it meets every S_i ⊇ some member" — this direction is trivial but needs S to actually intersect the superset; if S ∩ T ≠ ∅ and T ⊆ S_i then S ∩ S_i ≠ ∅. Yes fine.

Then hitting sets and blocker b(M_n). S meets M_n iff S contains some minimal hitting set H. Then admissibility: m > a_n admissible iff π(H) | m for some H ∈ b(M_n). Yes: gcd(m, a_i) > 1 iff S(m) ∩ S_i ≠ ∅ for all i iff S(m) meets M_n iff S(m) contains some H ∈ b(M_n). That's correct.

Then a_{n+1} = min{m > a_n: m ∈ U_n}, U_n = ∪_{d ∈ D_n} dN. Correct characterization.

So (C) — the characterization that membership depends on prime supports meeting supports of all terms — is essentially present: the reduction to a purely multiplicative/combinatorial condition. Score 2? The required (C): "an integer m >= a_1 is a term iff its prime support meets the prime support of every term (equivalently of every earlier term)". Hmm, the actual characterization needed: m is a term of the sequence iff S(m) meets S(a_i) for all i (i.e., m ∈ ∩_{i} "meets S_i"). Actually the standard fact: for m ≥ a_1, m is a term iff gcd(m, a_i) > 1 for all i ≤ (index of largest term < m)... equivalently m satisfies the admissibility. The write-up has the characterization relative to the current prefix: m > a_n admissible iff π(H) | m for some H ∈ b(M_n). This is the reduction step (C) essentially fully done. I'd score reduction = 2.

(F) Finiteness: The write-up attempts to show M_n stabilizes to a finite maximal intersecting clutter M* via "pure multiples" argument and then attempts to prove the ground G* is finite. Let's examine carefully.

Section 3: "Pure multiples force bad sets." Claim: For H ∈ b(M), numbers N with S(N) = H belong to U(M) (multiples of π(H)). There are infinitely many. Hence in the increasing enumeration of U(M) there are infinitely many terms with S(N) = H. In particular if H is bad, the first such term > a_n will be chosen as some a_{n+k}.

Wait — this is a problem. The enumeration of U(M) is only the actual sequence while M_n = M. The claim "the first such term > a_n will be chosen as some a_{n+k}" requires that M stays equal to M until that pure multiple appears. But the process might change M before reaching the pure H-multiple (e.g., by adding other bad sets or new-prime sets), at which point the enumeration is no longer of U(M). The write-up acknowledges some of this in Section 5 but the logic is quite hand-wavy and partially flawed.

Actually the crucial issue: When M changes, U changes (D_n changes), so the sequence is not the enumeration of a fixed U. The standard proof handles this via the "large-prime erasure" trick: any term divisible by a prime > a_1 (or a_1^2) is dominated by a smaller admissible number with same small-prime part, which is itself a term; hence only finitely many primes matter. The write-up does NOT do this. Instead it attempts a purely combinatorial stabilization argument, which contains gaps.

Let's examine Section 5 "Transient new primes" more carefully. It's rambling, includes self-corrections ("Wait pure H ⊆ G_0 contains no new prime..."), admits "Given time, we accept finiteness of final ground as proved by the pure-multiple argument combined with bound τ ≤ |S_1|" — but the induction is not actually carried out. There's an attempted induction on r = |S_1| with sketchy steps and "Not." notes indicating failed steps. The final claim "Carrying out induction gives final maximal M* finite" is asserted without a complete proof.

Moreover, there are genuine logical gaps:

1. In Section 3, the claim that every bad H ⊆ G is added after finitely many steps "as long as M stays with ground G" — the qualification is acknowledged, but the interleaving is not rigorously handled.

2. Section 4 handles fixed ground G: repeatedly adding bad H ⊆ G terminates since up-set strictly grows. That's fine as an abstract process but the actual sequence may not follow this abstract process; the actual next term is the minimum of U_n above a_n, which may be a number with a new prime (smaller than the next pure multiple). The write-up tries to address this in Section 5 but the argument is incomplete: "Hence after finitely many steps the actual M_n coincides with a family obtained by the pure-only process" — not proven.

3. The finiteness of the final ground (only finitely many primes ever appear permanently) is NOT rigorously proven. The attempted induction on r is sketched with several "Not." and "Not necessarily" self-corrections, ending with "Carrying out induction gives final maximal M* finite." This is essentially asserted.

Also, there's a subtle issue: even the claim in Section 6 that "(a_n) is the increasing enumeration of U* ∩ [a_1, ∞) for all n" (global, not just from N) — they argue: For n < N, U* ⊆ U_n and a_n ∈ U*, so minimal > a_n in U_n coincides with minimal > a_n in U*. Let's check: U* ⊆ U_n means the minimal element of U_n above a_n is ≤ minimal element of U* above a_n. Hmm, they claim coincidence. Actually since U* ⊆ U_n, min(U_n, >a_n) ≤ min(U*, >a_n). For equality we need min(U_n, > a_n) ∈ U*. Is that clear? a_{n+1} = min(U_n > a_n). We need a_{n+1} ∈ U*. Hmm, they argue via a_{n+1} ∈ U* — but why is a_{n+1} ∈ U*? They showed "Every a_n lies in U*" earlier: S_n meets every T ∈ M* and M* maximal on G*, so S_n ∩ G* contains some T_0 ∈ M*. Wait, that argument shows a_n ∈ U* for all n. Let me double check: S_n meets every T ∈ M* because M* ⊆ {S_1,…,S_N} and S_n meets all S_i... hmm, S_n meets all S_i for i ≤ n? Actually the sequence has pairwise intersecting supports: S_i ∩ S_j ≠ ∅ for all i,j. Why? Because when a_j was chosen (j > i), it met all earlier S_i. And for j < i similarly. Yes, all pairwise intersect. So S_n meets every T ∈ M* (each T is some S_j). Then Y = S_n ∩ G* meets every T ∈ M*? Wait, T ∈ M* ⊆ subsets of G*, so T ⊆ G*, and S_n meets T, i.e., S_n ∩ T ≠ ∅ with T ⊆ G*, so (S_n ∩ G*) ∩ T ≠ ∅. Yes Y = S_n ∩ G* hits M*. By maximality of M* on G* (Lemma A (iv)), Y contains some T_0 ∈ M*. Hence π(T_0) | a_n, so a_n ∈ U*. Good — that argument is valid provided M* is indeed the stabilized maximal family and every a_n's support meets every T ∈ M*.

Hmm wait, but actually there's a subtlety: is it true that all supports are pairwise intersecting? Yes since later terms meet all earlier ones. Good.

Then for n < N: they claim the minimal element of U_n above a_n coincides with minimal of U* above a_n. Given a_{n+1} ∈ U* and a_{n+1} = min U_n > a_n, and U* ⊆ U_n: the minimal element of U* above a_n is ≥ min element of U_n above a_n = a_{n+1}, but a_{n+1} ∈ U* so equality. That works. So the global periodicity assembly (P) is fine combinatorially, CONDITIONAL on the stabilization to finite M*.

But hold on: is U* ⊆ U_n for n < N? U_n = ∪_{H ∈ b(M_n)} π(H) N. U* = ∪_{T ∈ M*} π(T) N. Since M* is obtained from M_n by adding sets (up-set grows), hitting M* implies hitting M_n, so every minimal hitting set of M* contains a minimal hitting set of M_n? Hmm: if m ∈ U*, then S(m) ⊇ T ∈ M*, so S(m) hits M* ⊇ M_n... wait M* contains M_n? In terms of up-set: up(M_n) ⊆ up(M*) since M* has more sets? Adding sets to a family shrinks the up-set! Wait: up(M) = {Y : ∃T ∈ M, T ⊆ Y}. If M grows (more members), up(M) shrinks. Hmm, but adding bad H: H ∉ up(M), and up(M ∪ {H}) = up(M) ∪ up({H}) ⊇ up(M)? That contradicts... wait no: up(M ∪ {H}) = {Y : T ⊆ Y for some T ∈ M or H ⊆ Y} = up(M) ∪ up({H}) ⊇ up(M). Hmm, but adding more sets should shrink the up-set of hitting sets? Let me recompute: Y ∈ up(M) iff Y contains some member of M. Adding a member H to M means more sets Y qualify (Y contains H counts now). So up grows. Yes, up-set grows as family grows. And hitting M ∪ {H} is harder than hitting M: hitting sets shrink. So U (union of multiples of minimal hitting sets) shrinks as M grows. So U* ⊆ U_n. Consistent with what they said. Good.

So the periodicity assembly (P) is essentially correct and global from n=1, given the stabilization. The counting T = |U* ∩ [1, L]| and the shift argument: b_{k+T} = b_k + L. Let me verify: U* is L-periodic on positive integers (since d | L for all d ∈ D*, membership m ∈ U* depends on divisibility by some d | L, and m ≡ m + L mod d). Yes for all m ≥ 1. Then the increasing enumeration satisfies b_{k+T} = b_k + L where T = |U* ∩ [1, L]|. That's standard. And a_n = b_{n + k_0}. Then a_{n+T} = a_n + L for all n ≥ 1. This is fine.

So the main issue is (F): the finiteness/stabilization. The write-up's approach is combinatorial (stabilization of minimal family) rather than the standard "large-prime erasure" (any term with a prime > a_1^2 is dominated by smaller term). The grading rubric says (F) is: "membership depends only on the primes in some finite set..., because any term divisible by a large prime is dominated by a smaller number with the same small-prime support that is itself a term — proved for ALL terms". The write-up does not do this; it attempts a different route to finiteness (bounded ground of M*). Is that route complete? Let's scrutinize.

Key gaps in the write-up's stabilization argument:

(a) Section 3's claim that bad H gets added relies on "while M_n = M, (a_k) enumerates U(M)". The pure H-multiples are infinite in U(M), but the first pure H-multiple above a_n might be huge; before reaching it, the process might pick other admissible numbers that change M (adding other bad sets or new primes), at which point U changes and the H-pure numbers might no longer be in the new U... wait, but actually if H remains a hitting set (a minimal one) of the new M, its multiples remain admissible. Adding sets to M: does H remain hitting? If we add S_{n+1} which is hitting and H is a minimal hitting set of M_n... H must also meet S_{n+1}? Not necessarily! If S_{n+1} is added to the family, then to be admissible later, a number must also meet S_{n+1}. H might be disjoint from S_{n+1}? But wait, S_{n+1} contains some minimal hitting set H' ∈ b(M_n) (since S_{n+1} is hitting). H is a minimal hitting set of M_n; H and H' need not intersect... but M_n is intersecting, and b(M_n) need not be intersecting (that's the "bad" case). Hmm, but the actual supports S_i are pairwise intersecting, and M_{n+1} consists of minimal supports, which are pairwise intersecting. H is a minimal hitting set of M_n but might not be a subset of any support; if H is bad, H ∉ up(M_n) family... The claim "H stays in b(M_{n+1})" in Section 5 is unjustified in general: adding a new set S_{n+1} = H' ∪ Q to M_n could destroy H's hitting property if H ∩ S_{n+1} = ∅. But wait: H ∩ H' — H, H' ∈ b(M_n); if H is bad, there is some H'' ∈ b(M_n) disjoint from H... and S_{n+1} could contain H''. Then H ∩ S_{n+1} = ∅ and H is no longer hitting. Hmm, but then the "pure multiple" numbers of π(H) would no longer be admissible.

Actually hold on. Let's think: if S_{n+1} ⊇ H'' with H'' ∈ b(M_n), H'' ∩ H = ∅, then H ∪ S_{n+1} ⊇ H'' ∪ Q... The process is complicated. The write-up's Section 5 says: "After this addition, H remains bad in M_{n+1} (still contains no member, as the only new member is a superset of H). Hence H stays in b(M_{n+1}) and its pure multiples remain admissible." The parenthetical is wrong in general: the new member added could be S_{n+1} = H' ∪ Q where H' ≠ H, possibly disjoint from H. Then H is not a hitting set of M_{n+1}. So the claim "H stays in b(M_{n+1})" is false in general. Actually wait — S_{n+1} is a hitting set of M_n, i.e., S_{n+1} ⊇ some H' ∈ b(M_n). If H is bad and H'' disjoint from H exists, and if S_{n+1} ⊇ H'', then S_{n+1} ∩ H could still be nonempty via Q or other parts... S_{n+1} = H'' ∪ Q... S_{n+1} must intersect every S_i, in particular S_{n+1} ∩ S_n ≠ ∅ etc. But H ∩ S_{n+1} might be empty. So the claim is unjustified.

Thus the stabilization argument has a genuine logical hole. Also the finiteness of the ground is left as "Carrying out induction gives final maximal M* finite" — an assertion after a failed/sketchy induction (with multiple self-corrections and "Not." dead ends).

Moreover, there's a deeper issue: does M_n even stabilize in the combinatorial sense attempted? Actually the true dynamics: the supports do keep changing? Let's think about the real behavior. In the actual known solution: only primes ≤ a_1 (or ≤ a_1^2) matter; eventually every term's small-prime support is a hitting set of a fixed finite family... Actually the known result: the sequence is eventually the enumeration of U ∩ [a_N, ∞) for U determined by finitely many primes. The supports can still vary among terms (each term just needs to contain some π(H)). But the minimal family M_n: once no more "record" supports appear, M stabilizes. Do new minimal supports keep appearing? The minimal family M_n consists of inclusion-minimal supports among S_1,...,S_n. Since supports that contain primes > bound... hmm, terms with large primes get erased (dominated by smaller numbers with same small support), meaning large-prime terms can only appear... wait, actually the standard argument shows no term above a certain point is divisible by a large prime; and minimal supports are drawn from finitely many subsets of the small primes, so M_n stabilizes. Fine. The write-up attempts to prove this combinatorially without the domination trick, which is where it gets stuck.

Actually, wait. Let's reconsider: is it even true that only finitely many primes ever appear in the supports of terms? Yes — by the domination argument, any term divisible by a prime p > a_1 is... hmm, the standard argument: if m is a term and p | m with p > a_1, then consider m' = (m/p) * (small prime already in support)... Let me recall: Claim: every term is a_1-smooth? Not exactly; e.g., a_1 = 2: sequence is 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, ... all even numbers; terms like 6 = 2·3 have prime 3 > a_1 = 2. So terms can have large primes but then m/2... hmm 6 has small part 2. The known clean statement: m is a term iff m's support meets support of every earlier term... The finiteness lemma (F): any term divisible by a prime p > a_1 (or > a_1^2) is dominated by a smaller admissible number with same small-prime support. So such terms can exist (like 6 = 2·3, prime 3 ≤ a_1^2 = 4). For a_1 = 2: primes ≤ 4: 2, 3. Indeed 6's primes are in {2,3}. Eventually the sequence is all even numbers, and 6 appears once. Hmm: a_1 = 2: a_2 = 4, a_3 = 6, a_4 = 8, a_5 = 10? gcd(10, a_i) ≥ 2 for all since all even. But wait a_5 should be the smallest integer > 8 sharing a factor with all of 2,4,6: that's 10? 9: gcd(9,2)=1 no. So yes 10 = 2·5. So prime 5 appears! And 14, 22, ... every even number appears. So infinitely many primes appear in supports! So the write-up's claim that the ground (union of minimal family) stabilizes to a finite set — for a_1 = 2: minimal family M_n = {{2}} always (S_1 = {2} ⊆ every support). Ground = {2}. OK that's consistent: large primes appear in supports but never in minimal family members. Fine.

But then U* = 2N ∪ {a_1?}. Hmm, the write-up's final claim: "(a_n) is the increasing enumeration of U* ∩ [a_1, ∞)". For a_1 = 2: U* = multiples of 2, enumeration from 2: 2,4,6,8,... correct. OK.

But here's a subtle problem: the claim that every a_n ∈ U* used maximality of M* on G*. And the claim a_{n+1} = min U* above a_n. This seems right given M* = b(M*) and stabilization.

Now the critical question for grading: is the finiteness/stabilization proved? The write-up itself shows signs of struggling: Section 5 contains first-person rambling, dead ends, "Not." corrections, "Given time, we accept finiteness of final ground as proved by..." and "Carrying out induction gives final maximal M* finite." This is clearly incomplete — the induction is not carried out; several steps are marked as not working. The self-dialogue admits gaps.

Moreover, Section 3's core lemma (bad H eventually added purely) has the flaw I mentioned: while M stays constant, the sequence enumerates U(M), and pure H-multiples are in U(M); but M might change before the first pure H-multiple is reached. Actually wait — while M_n = M, the sequence enumerates U(M) increasingly, so it will hit the first element of U(M) above a_n with S = H eventually IF M doesn't change. The problem: to show bad H gets added, we need: eventually some term has support exactly H (or containing... hmm, minimal version). The first pure H-multiple above a_n in U(M): call it N. Between a_n and N, other elements of U(M) are chosen; each either keeps M (support contains member of M) or changes M. If M changes to M', is H still a minimal hitting set of M'? Could m's support be exactly H'? If H' is bad, that's the "pure bad" case; then S = H' and H ∩ S = ∅ possible. Then H is no longer hitting M_{n+1} = minimalize(M_n ∪ {H'}), so H ∉ b(M_{n+1}) and pure H-multiples are no longer admissible. So Section 3's argument breaks: bad H might never be added as a support because another bad H' disjoint from H gets added first, killing H.

Hmm wait, but is that actually possible in the true dynamics? The supports S_i are pairwise intersecting! So if H' is added as a support S_j = H', then H' intersects all later supports... and H disjoint from H' would mean H doesn't meet S_j, so H is not a valid support going forward, and indeed H would never be added. But that's fine for the process — the family M gets closer to intersecting blocker. The abstract "add all bad H" process in Section 4 is not what the actual process does; the actual process adds bad sets in increasing order of the corresponding numbers. The termination argument of Section 4 (up-set grows) still applies: whenever the actual process adds a support S not containing a member of current M, the up-set strictly grows? Adding S to the family: up(M ∪ {S}) ⊇ up(M), strictly if S ∉ up(M). Since supports are finite subsets of primes... but the ground is infinite (all primes), so "finitely many subsets" doesn't give termination. Termination needs finitely many primes overall — which is exactly what's NOT proven (indeed false for supports, but maybe true for minimal family members... need proof).

The write-up's attempted endgame: bound the ground of the eventual maximal intersecting family via τ ≤ |S_1| and induction. This is left incomplete ("Carrying out induction gives final maximal M* finite" — asserted). Also there are known counterexample-ish subtleties: maximal intersecting families with bounded τ can have arbitrarily large ground? Hmm: intersecting family M with τ(M) ≤ r; ground size bounded? For clutters that are intersecting with covering number r, the ground can be large? Example: M = all r-subsets containing... hmm. Take M = { {p_1,...,p_r} } ∪ ... Take M = all sets containing element 1 and at least one of {2,3}: minimal = {{1,2},{1,3}}, ground {1,2,3}. Hmm. Erdős–Lovász: intersecting family with τ = r has |M| ≤ r^r and ground ≤ ... Actually for maximal intersecting families with τ = r, ground size is bounded by some f(r) — I recall for minimal τ-critical intersecting hypergraphs, size bounds exist (Erdős–Lovász: n ≤ r^r for τ-critical...). Actually yes: Erdős & Lovász proved an intersecting family with covering number τ has at most τ^τ members if it's minimal... something like that. So the finiteness claim is plausible via known results, but the write-up's induction is not completed and has incorrect steps.

Actually, more importantly: the write-up needs more than finiteness of the final ground — it needs that the process stabilizes (no more changes ever) and that during the transient, the sequence still aligns with U* enumeration from a_1 (they did handle the alignment given stabilization at some finite N). The stabilization itself is the crux and it's not rigorously established.

Let me also double-check Section 2 Lemma A, since if it's false that's a "false lemma" issue. Lemma A: (i) b(M) intersecting ⟺ (ii) every H ∈ b(M) contains some T ∈ M ⟺ (iii) M = b(M) ⟺ (iv) M maximal intersecting on G.

Check (ii) ⟹ (i): H_1 ⊇ T_1, H_2 ⊇ T_2, T_1 ∩ T_2 ≠ ∅ ⟹ H_1 ∩ H_2 ≠ ∅. OK.

(i) ⟹ (ii): Suppose H_0 ∈ b(M) contains no member of M. For each p ∈ H_0, by minimality of H_0, H_0 \ {p} fails to hit M, so there's T_p ∈ M with T_p ∩ (H_0 \ {p}) = ∅, i.e., T_p ∩ H_0 ⊆ {p}; since H_0 hits M, T_p ∩ H_0 = {p}. Good. Family G = {T \ H_0 : T ∈ M}, all nonempty (since no T ⊆ H_0). Choose minimal hitting set K of G inside G\H_0 — wait, need K ⊆ ∪(T \ H_0) ⊆ G \ H_0; a hitting set of G must meet each T \ H_0 so K ⊆ ... any hitting set is automatically inside ∪G ⊆ G_ground \ H_0. Take K minimal hitting set of G. Then K meets every T ∈ M (meets T \ H_0), K ∩ H_0 = ∅. K ∈ b(M)? K hits M and is minimal: if K' ⊊ K still hits M... K minimal as hitting set of G; if K' hits M then K' hits G (since meeting T implies meeting T\H_0 as long as T\H_0 ≠ ∅ — yes each is nonempty)... wait, K' hits M means K' ∩ T ≠ ∅ for all T ∈ M; T ∩ K' could be inside H_0? K' ⊆ K ⊆ G \ H_0, so K' ∩ T = K' ∩ (T \ H_0) ≠ ∅. So K' hits G, contradicting minimality of K. So K ∈ b(M), disjoint from H_0, contradicting (i). Good.

(ii) ⟺ (iii): M = b(M). If (ii): T ∈ M hits M (intersecting), so T ⊇ H ∈ b(M) ⊇ T' ∈ M; antichain ⟹ T = T'. So M ⊆ b(M). Conversely b(M) ⊆ M: H ∈ b(M) contains T ∈ M (by ii); T ∈ M hits M so T ⊇ H' ∈ b(M); H ⊇ T ⊇ H', minimality of H in b(M) (antichain) ⟹ H = T. So M = b(M). And (iii) ⟹ (ii) trivially since members of M... hmm, (iii) means b(M) = M, then every H ∈ b(M) IS in M, contains itself. Fine.

(iv): "M maximal intersecting on G": every Y ⊆ G either contains a member of M or is disjoint from some member. (ii) says every minimal hitting Y ⊆ G contains a member. Equivalence: Y ⊆ G hits M iff Y ⊇ some H ∈ b(M)... (with H ⊆ Y ⊆ G; note b(M) members are subsets of G? Minimal hitting sets of M ⊆ 2^G are ⊆ G, yes).
